newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks seen gaining in fiscal 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks seen gaining in fiscal 1997/98.

text.p: Pakistani investors are hoping that Friday's budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) will help revitalise the economy and boost flagging equities.

Analysts said they expected few surprises in Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz's budget because the government had already set out its economic revival programme in tax and tariff cuts and other incentive packages announced earlier.

"Nobody is expecting miracles from this government, but at least the recent economic reforms and packages are in the right direction, which will help stocks," said Farooq Lakhani, country manager of International Asset Management Co Ltd.
"But it will take time before these polices begin to pay dividends," he added.
He said the budget was likely to be along the same lines as the export-oriented measures announced in March and April after Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif captured power in February 3 polls.
These were designed to develop capital markets, help the agriculture and textile sectors, and reform the banking sector.
Analysts said stocks would benefit as Sharif's policies begin to have an effect over the next one or two years.

Wahid Butt, chief analyst at Carr Mashriq, said stock prices had fallen in 1996/97 due to heavy taxes in the budget. "This year, sentiment is likely to remain positive as the government has announced that it will not impose new taxes," he said.
Trading volume at the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) has shrunk and prices have tumbled this year because of Pakistan's economic troubles and past political instability, dealers say.
The KSE 100-share index sank below 1,500 points early this month from the year-high of 1,775.57 on February 20, but a pre-budget rally pushed it over 1,600 points on Tuesday.
Dealer Dawar Hasan of Global Securities said the rally was overdue because the index had slipped to attractive levels.
"The market is riding on sentiment in pre-budget days. If the index retains 30 to 40 percent of its recent gains it would be good for the market," Lakhani said.
Sameer Ahmed, chief dealer at ING Baring, said stock prices were unlikely to surge after the budget because the government's supply side economic policy would have a delayed impact.
"There will be a gradual turn-round in stocks as the economy revives in response to recent policies," he said.
He said second-tier scrips were likely to slip on selling pressure after the budget, while blue chips would remain firm, assuming Aziz springs no nasty surprises.
"But there are fears that local institutions would again be sellers at higher levels," Ahmed added.
Last month KSE president Arif Habib identified the activity of local institutions as one factor depressing stock prices.
"On average local institutions invest seven to eight billion rupees ($173 to $198 million) every year in stocks...but this year they have disinvested about six billion rupees," he said.
He said there were expectations that the budget would cut excise duty in sectors such as telecommunications and cement.

Butt said investors had stopped buying shares earlier in the year on fears of possible policy U-turns. "These concerns have died down as the government remains committed to its reforms in line with IMF directives," he said. "After the budget, macro-economic indicators will drive the market."
Lakhani said the government should slash spending, but any cuts in the development budget would hamper growth.
"If there is no investment in infrastructure development, it would mean a definite slowdown in the economy," he said.
However, he said government plans to cut bank borrowing and reduce interest rates would free liquidity in the banking system which would boost business, investment and company profits.
"In terms of value, the Pakistani market is cheap and investors could take their cue from the budget," Lakhani added.
